document.abstract: The Image Interchange Framework (IIF), created by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences with the goal of providing a unified post-production workflow, has seen increased interest in recent years. Central to the IIF is the red, green, and blue wide-gamut color space defined by the Academy of Color Encoding Specification (ACES). For output device viewing, the ACES data must first be rendered through the reference rendering transform (RRT) and the output device transform (ODT). Recently, a quasi-logarithmic 12-bit integer ACES encoding scheme was proposed, and initial results are presented on the direct display of integer ACES content on a Dolby PRM-4200 monitor. Frames were delivered directly to the monitor across a 12-bit dual-link serial digital interface, and the decoding RRT and device ODT were computed via one- and three-dimensional (3D) lookup tables (LUTs) resident on the monitor. Several LUT designs were considered, and the limitations of each, including failure modes, are discussed.

authors.bio: Jon McElvain is currently with the Image Tech Research division of Dolby Laboratories, based in Burbank, CA. He specializes in camera and display systems, image quality quantification, and image processing algorithm development. His previous positions were with Digital Imaging Systems GmbH, Micron Inc. (imaging division, now Aptina) and with Xerox Corp. He has more than 20 publications and holds 24 patents, with another 12 patents pending. He is a member of SMPTE, IS&T and IEEE, and is the past-chair of the IEEE Standing Committee on Industry Signal Processing Technology (IDSP). McElvain received a B.S. in physics from the University of California, San Diego; a M.A. in physics from the University of California, Berkeley; and a Ph.D. in physics from the University of California, Santa Barbara.
authors.name: Jon S. McElvain

authors.bio: David Ruhoff is a senior staff engineer in the Image Technology Research department at Dolby Laboratories. He has more than 30 years of software development experience in diverse applications such as logic simulation and compilers. Since 1982, he has focused on computer graphics, film scanning and recording, video, and compression. In 1984, he received screen credit for his work on The Last Starfighter, one of the first full-length motion pictures to use extensive CGI. In 1996, he received an Academy Technical Achievement Award for pioneering efforts in the creation of the Digital Film Compositing System at Digital Productions.
authors.name: David Ruhoff

authors.bio: Glenn Woodruff is a project engineer at Dolby Laboratories, concentrating on color engineering, video processing, and monitoring. Before joining Dolby, Woodruff was Employee #1 at Cine-tal Systems and has previously held positions with Truevision and Pinnacle Systems. He received a B.S.E.E. degree from Purdue University in 1997.
authors.name: Glenn Woodruff

authors.bio: Walter Gish is principal member at Dolby's Image Technology Research and Development group, where he leads research and development efforts for next-generation imaging technology. He has more than 30 years of experience in signal and image processing, high-performance computing, and hardware development. Gish began his career working on classified (Top Secret) sonar, radar, and image analysis applications for the U.S. government. Since the early 1980s he has focused on computer graphics, video, and display technology. Prior to joining Dolby Laboratories he was Principal Engineer at Evans & Sutherland, executive scientist at Terabit, and chief technology officer at Interactive Machines, Inc. — Gish received screen credit for his work on The Last Starfighter, the first full-length motion picture to use extensive CGI. He received special recognition from ISO/IEC for his contributions to the development of the High Profiles for H.264/AVC, which were awarded an Emmy in 2008. His current interests include compression algorithms, high dynamic range and wide color gamut imaging technology, and forensic watermarking. Gish received a B.S. and M.S. in physics and applied mathematics from the California Institute of Technology in 1968 and 1970, respectively.
authors.name: Walter Gish

authors.bio: Dave Schnuelle represents Dolby Laboratories as senior director, image technology, and is responsible for guidance in Dolby's efforts in the television, cinema, and consumer imaging areas. He began his career as an engineer on television outside broadcasts while attending Purdue University. Schnuelle later held positions as chief engineer at various post-production facilities such as Editel and Modern VideoFilm in Los Angeles.
authors.name: David Schnuelle
